```go
func TestParseWikilinks_MdNormalizationProperty(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	rapid.Check(t, func(rt *rapid.T) {

		name := rapid.StringMatching(`[0-9]+[a-z0-9]*\.[a-z0-9-]+`).Draw(rt, "name")
```

Failing case: `name` = `"0.md"` (a valid draw — `[0-9]+[a-z0-9]*\.[a-z0-9-]+` matches "0" + "." + "md"). Then:
- `bare = ParseWikilinks("[[0.md]]")` → `ParseWikilinks` strips one trailing `.md` → `["0"]`

# Findings: CPU-only llama.cpp tuning for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on M1 Pro 16GB

## Ranked recommendations

**1. Highest payoff: stop re-prefilling history — server-side prompt caching (free, addresses the pi-agent pattern directly)**
- llama-server does exact-prefix KV reuse per slot by default (`cache_prompt` defaults to true in the API). For an agent that only *appends* to a byte-stable prefix, this alone eliminates re-prefill of prior turns — the growing-history cost drops to prefilling only the new turn. Requirement: the prefix must be byte-identical each turn (no timestamp, no re-serialized system prompt, sampler/template identical). See the [KV cache reuse tutorial (discussion #13606)](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/13606) and the [Claude Code prompt-cache-killer writeup](https://www.mykolaaleksandrov.dev/posts/2026/06/claude-code-llamacpp-prompt-cache-fix/) — the usual failure is a mutating prefix, not the cache.
- `--cache-reuse 256` additionally enables KV-shift reuse of *partial* matches, but there is an open regression report ([issue #15082](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/15082)) that it stopped working in some builds; verify with `n_past` in server logs rather than trusting the flag. For deterministic cross-restart persistence use `--slot-save-path` + the `/slots/{id}?action=save|restore` API ([discussion #18244](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/18244), [7minai guide](https://7minai.com/how-to-fix-llama-server-kv-cache-reuse/)). Run with `--parallel 1` so requests always land in the same slot (default slot selection is similarity-based, `-sps 0.5`).

**2. The 10.6→5.5 drop at 5k ctx is probably memory pressure, not attention cost — shrink `-c` (high confidence, verify locally)**
- Qwen3.6-A3B is hybrid: most layers are Gated DeltaNet with *fixed-size* recurrent state; only a minority are full attention ([Unsloth Qwen3-Next guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/tutorials/qwen3-next)). So per-token attention cost grows only in those few layers — a ~2x decode drop at just 5k tokens is too steep to be attention arithmetic. *Speculation, but well-grounded:* with a 17GB mmap'd file on 16GB RAM, a growing KV/state + compute buffers evict mmap'd expert pages, and decode becomes SSD-page-fault-bound. Test: run with `-c 8192` instead of 32768 (KV allocation shrinks), watch `memory_pressure`/pageins during long-ctx decode. If pageins spike, that's the cause; a smaller `-c` plus KV quant recovers most of it.
- `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` helps here mainly by shrinking the resident footprint (less eviction of weights), secondarily by KV bandwidth. Only applies to the full-attention layers; DeltaNet state is unaffected. Note `-ctv` quant requires flash attention, which you already have on.

**3. Partial Metal offload IS possible without wiring the whole file: `-ngl 99 --cpu-moe` (worth testing, moderate confidence)**
- Metal only wires the buffers assigned to it. `--cpu-moe` (or `-n-cpu-moe N`, or `--override-tensor "\.ffn_.*_exps\.=CPU"`) keeps all routed-expert tensors on CPU (still mmap'd/pageable) while attention, norms, shared expert, and output go to Metal. For an A3B model the non-expert tensors are small (order 1–2GB at Q3/Q4), so wired memory stays far below 16GB. This is the standard MoE hybrid recipe ([HF MoE offload guide](https://huggingface.co/blog/Doctor-Shotgun/llamacpp-moe-offload-guide), [DocShotgun gist](https://gist.github.com/DocShotgun/a02a4c0c0a57e43ff4f038b46ca66ae0), [-ot discussion #13154](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/13154)). Expected win: attention (the part that grows with context) runs on GPU, and prefill gets meaningfully faster; expert matmuls stay CPU-bound. This directly attacks both your prefill number and the context-decay slope. Caveat (*speculation*): on unified memory the win is smaller than on discrete GPUs, and the Metal/GDN kernel support for this arch must exist in your build — just benchmark `llama-bench -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe`-style A/B.
- Bleeding edge, not merged: [RFC/PoC discussion #23324](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/23324) — MoE disk offload with on-demand expert paging on Metal (LRU slot pool, `pread` sidecar). Measured Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q6_K on M3 Pro: 15.7–29.1 tok/s depending on slots; reported running on an **M1 Pro 16GB at ~13 tok/s**. Requires `--no-mmap --no-warmup` and a branch build. Watch this; it's exactly your hardware scenario.
- Also open: [issue #20757](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/20757), two-tier expert cache feature request — not implemented.

**4. Prefill: `-ub`/`-b` tuning, and confirm your build uses Accelerate**
- Larger `-ub` helps prefill on Metal substantially; on pure CPU the gain is smaller but real up to a point — try `-ub 512/1024/2048 -b 2048` with `llama-bench -p 2048`. Cost is compute-buffer RAM, which matters at 16GB ([starmorph guide](https://blog.starmorph.com/blog/apple-silicon-llm-inference-optimization-guide), [tuning llama-server on Apple Silicon](https://medium.com/@michael.hannecke/tuning-llama-server-on-apple-silicon-9b3e778ab100)).
- Apple AMX: llama.cpp reaches AMX only indirectly via the Accelerate framework BLAS path (`GGML_ACCELERATE`/`GGML_BLAS=Accelerate`, on by default in macOS builds) — it accelerates large-matrix prefill GEMMs, not decode GEMVs. Check your build log for `BLAS = 1 / Accelerate`. There is no dedicated Apple-AMX ggml backend. If you built with plain `cmake` flags disabled, rebuilding with Accelerate is free prefill speed. If experts are quantized, BLAS is bypassed for those matmuls (dequant cost), so effect may be modest — measure.

**5. Threads: `-t 8` (P-cores only); skip `--numa`**
- Community guidance and the [M-series performance megathread (discussion #4167)](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/4167) consistently show best results with threads = P-core count; adding E-cores (`-t 10`) causes straggler sync stalls and often *reduces* tok/s. macOS has no user cpu-pinning (`--cpu-mask` is Linux-effective; macOS ignores affinity), and `--numa` is a no-op on single-die Apple Silicon. Set `-t 8 -tb 8`, done. Decode is bandwidth-bound anyway (~200GB/s ceiling).

**6. Quant switch to Q4_0 + runtime repack: probably NOT a win for decode**
- llama.cpp now repacks Q4_0 automatically at load into interleaved ARM formats (the old Q4_0_4_4/4_8 types were removed — [issue #10757](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/10757), [issue #12701](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/12701) notes server-side quirks). This *does* apply to CPU-only runs on Apple Silicon (`-ngl 0`); the "not for Apple Silicon" advice assumes Metal use. M1 has NEON dotprod but no i8mm, so it gets the 4x4 path only (*i8mm arrived with M2 — moderate confidence*). Repack mainly speeds **prefill** (GEMM); **decode** is bandwidth-bound, and Q4_0 is ~20-25% more bytes than UD-Q3_K_XL — on a machine already paging a 17GB file, bigger is worse. Verdict: keep UD-Q3_K_XL; if anything, test a *smaller* quant (UD-Q2_K_XL / IQ3) to reduce paging — likely a larger real-world win than kernel micro-optimizations (*speculation, measure*).

**7. ik_llama.cpp fork: real CPU gains, use with eyes open**
- [ik_llama.cpp](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp) is actively maintained, GGUF-compatible, with fused MoE ops (`-fmoe`), `-rtr` runtime repack, and generally best-in-class CPU prompt-processing speed; its own docs warn against `-rtr` in hybrid CPU/GPU setups ([hybrid docs](https://ikawrakow-ik_llama-cpp.mintlify.app/inference/hybrid-cpu-gpu), [parameters](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/blob/main/docs/parameters.md)). For pure CPU it's a legitimate option — CPU prefill gains of 1.5-3x are commonly reported for MoE. Risks: lags mainline on brand-new architectures — verify it supports the Qwen3.6 hybrid GDN arch before investing (*unverified for this specific model*). There's also a further fork ([firecoperana/ik_llama.cpp_fcp](https://github.com/firecoperana/ik_llama.cpp_fcp)).

## Suggested experiment order
1. `-c 8192 -t 8 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0`, single slot, verify prefix cache hits in server logs (biggest wall-clock win for the pi loop).
2. A/B `-ngl 99 --cpu-moe` vs `-ngl 0` with `llama-bench` (pp2048 + tg128 at depth 4096).
3. `-ub` sweep for prefill; confirm Accelerate in build.
4. Try a smaller quant to escape paging.
5. Optionally trial ik_llama.cpp and track discussion #23324.

Sources: [starmorph Apple Silicon guide](https://blog.starmorph.com/blog/apple-silicon-llm-inference-optimization-guide), [HF MoE offload guide](https://huggingface.co/blog/Doctor-Shotgun/llamacpp-moe-offload-guide), [discussion #4167](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/4167), [discussion #13606](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/13606), [issue #15082](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/15082), [discussion #18244](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/18244), [discussion #23324](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/23324), [issue #20757](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/20757), [discussion #13154](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/13154), [DocShotgun gist](https://gist.github.com/DocShotgun/a02a4c0c0a57e43ff4f038b46ca66ae0), [issue #10757](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/10757), [issue #12701](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/12701), [ik_llama.cpp](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp), [ik hybrid docs](https://ikawrakow-ik_llama-cpp.mintlify.app/inference/hybrid-cpu-gpu), [Unsloth Qwen3-Next](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/tutorials/qwen3-next), [maloyan 16GB M4 writeup](https://maloyan.xyz/blog/running-qwen-locally-mac-mini-m4), [7minai KV cache guide](https://7minai.com/how-to-fix-llama-server-kv-cache-reuse/), [Mykola Aleksandrov prompt-cache post](https://www.mykolaaleksandrov.dev/posts/2026/06/claude-code-llamacpp-prompt-cache-fix/)

  --predicate "breaks internal DNS in every machine, and the public URLs keep working so it looks fine" \
  --object "measured 2026-08-03: after 'orbctl stop', /etc/resolv.conf in every env contained ONLY tailscale MagicDNS (nameserver 100.100.100.100 + fd7a:115c:a1e0::53) with no fallback, so host.orb.internal AND ordinary public DNS both failed inside the envs. systemd-resolved was inactive, so tailscale took the file over in direct mode and dropped OrbStack's resolver. Tailscale keeps the original at /etc/resolv.pre-tailscale-backup.conf, which reveals the right value: 'nameserver 0.250.250.200' (OrbStack's resolver, routed via the orb gateway). SYMPTOMS ARE MISLEADING: public app URLs stayed 200/302 throughout because ingress is INBOUND over the tailnet and needs no DNS inside the env; what broke was anything the env initiates — the dashboard's proxy to apphostd returned 502, and pi could not reach the model service. curl exits 6 (couldn't resolve), not 7 (refused), which distinguishes this from a service being down. FIX THAT WORKED: inside each env, 'tailscale set --accept-dns=false', then replace /etc/resolv.conf with 'nameserver 0.250.250.200' + 'options edns0' + 'search .', then restart the app unit if its process caches a resolved address. (2) vault note 651 (openspec-modified-blocks-carry-all-base-scenarios) is an archive-time enforcement (openspec archive checks it), not an edit-time one — a plan that gates a single-sentence spec edit on full scenario-header parity against the live spec over-applies it, especially when the mismatch traces to an unrelated orphaned uncommitted diff from a third change; learn_calls.skill_args: Mid-cycle fast path, single confirmed correction. Context: implementing phone-llm's integrations-run-inside-the-app. A live verification test (task 4.4) caught a real defect: app_services() — a READ path — correctly classified a substituted service on a registered port as "IDENTITY CHANGED" and rendered the per-signal diff, but left the ingress route up and the unix socket serving the substitute. The fail-closed enforcement lived only in verify_integration(), which nothing on the read path called. So the platform detected the confused-deputy state, displayed a warning about it, and went on serving an unknown service under a registered name and inside its Access gate. Confirmed by live measurement, then reproduced as a RED unit test, then fixed by extracting _enforce_identity() and calling it from BOTH app_services() and verify_integration(). Lesson: when a classification identifies a security-relevant state, the code path that OBSERVES it must also ACT on it — a read that only reports the state has not failed closed, it has narrated. Splitting detection (a read) from enforcement (a separate function) leaves a window where the platform knows and serves anyway. Corollary confirmed in the same session: unit tests + a 5-mutation check all passed while this defect was live; only the end-to-end substitution test on real infrastructure found it.

HANDOFF from learn (mid-cycle, self-discovered reversal).

**ACK on actionability.** The seven-item spec is now sufficient for an executor to write without returning to the current design.md for synthesis. Each point is specific: claim, evidence, or consequence.

One minor note on *internal consistency*: Items 3–5 work together but could confuse an executor if read separately.

- Item 3 asserts "This is the enforcement" (pointing to loopback bind blocking machine-to-machine)
- Item 4 states what the ACL buys (governs tailnet plane against tailnet peers)  
- Item 5's table slots machine-to-machine as "**nothing; only not-listening**" and tailnet-to-tailnet as "the ACL"

An executor reading linearly would see: *"This is the enforcement"* → *"what the ACL does buy"* → *"table showing two different enforcement pictures"* and need to hold both: the loopback bind blocks machine-to-machine; the ACL blocks tailnet-to-tailnet. It's stated, but the logical relationship ("enforcement for different planes") is implicit.

Not blockers — the individual claims are clear. Just: a reader unfamiliar with the substrate might momentarily think item 3 and item 4 are in tension. The spec stands.

**ACK on register.** Correct distinction: the plan is a coordination checklist; prose belongs in the decision being written. The disposition table's terseness is appropriate; Gate A's reviewer will see the same terse row and will verify it against the written artifact. That's a separate gate. Retracted.

## Verification Report — A1 bypass-fixture plan (revised)

Method: read the plan and both live source files in full; additionally wrote isolated dash (strict POSIX sh) reproductions of the exact trap snippet and ran them under real signals, and simulated the awk single-source-of-truth extraction against the real `appctl_lib.py` content, rather than reasoning about shell semantics from memory.

### 1. POSIX sh trap mechanism (§3) — holds structurally, but has one real gap

Confirmed via `dash -n` (syntax) and two live runs under `dash` with a stubbed `orb`:

- **Happy path** (no interrupt): `bypass_active` as a plain (non-`local`) variable is correctly shared between the top-level block and `bypass_cleanup()` — no subshell separates them, and it's assigned (`bypass_active=0`) before the trap is armed, so `set -u` never sees it unbound. The manual `bypass_cleanup` call followed by `trap - EXIT INT TERM` disarms cleanly: cleanup ran exactly once, no double-fire at script exit. This part of the plan holds.

- **Interrupt path** — this is the real finding. I sent `kill -TERM` to a running instance of the exact snippet mid-"probe":
```
sleeping...
cleanup ran
AFTER SLEEP - script resumed instead of terminating
exit code: 0
```
`trap bypass_cleanup EXIT INT TERM` **restores state correctly** (tailscaled restarted, fixture stopped — the safety property the plan exists to guarantee does hold). But because `bypass_cleanup` never calls `exit`, POSIX/dash trap semantics mean the shell **does not terminate on SIGINT/SIGTERM** — it resumes execution right after the interrupted command and runs the rest of `check-isolation` to completion as if nothing happened. A Ctrl-C or `kill` during the bypass section will not actually stop the check; it'll look like the interrupt did nothing.

This is a real, verified gap, not the same one already fixed (state restoration works fine). The plan's own §6 test ("confirm the trap actually restores tailscaled and stops the fixture") won't catch it, because it only checks restoration, not termination.

**What better looks like:** separate the EXIT trap from the INT/TERM traps, and have the latter explicitly exit after cleanup:
```sh
trap bypass_cleanup EXIT
trap 'bypass_cleanup; trap - INT TERM; kill -$$ ...; exit 130' INT TERM
```
(or the simpler idiom: `trap 'bypass_cleanup; exit 130' INT TERM` plus `trap bypass_cleanup EXIT`, being mindful that `exit` inside the INT/TERM handler re-fires the EXIT trap — harmless here since `bypass_cleanup` is idempotent on `bypass_active=0`, but worth a comment so it isn't "fixed" into an infinite loop later).

### 2. `getent hosts` inside golden — holds (narrow question), with a bigger caveat worth surfacing

`bin/build-golden`'s package list (`python3 python3-venv git curl ca-certificates build-essential nodejs npm less jq fish`) never installs `getent` explicitly — correctly so: `getent` ships in `libc-bin`, `Priority: required`/`Essential: yes` on every Debian/Ubuntu base, including OrbStack's `ubuntu` cloud image. No network install needed; the plan's assumption of availability is safe.

Bigger unaddressed risk, surfaced because it bears directly on whether §6's "expected right now" claims will actually hold: MagicDNS resolution for `*.$TAILNET` names is served by `tailscaled` itself (typically via a stub resolver wired to 100.100.100.100). The DNS check runs *after* `systemctl stop tailscaled`. It's plausible `getent hosts other.$TAILNET` will fail to resolve for **every** neighbour once tailscaled is down — not because of any ACL property, but because the resolver process is gone — which would make the DNS-first `fail`/`continue` fire on every iteration and never actually exercise `denied()`/`ssh_blocked()` for the HTTP/SSH plane at all. To the plan's credit, §6 already treats "confirm the DNS check passes for every real app" as something to verify live rather than assume, and fails loudly rather than silently if it doesn't — so this isn't an unhandled gap in process, but it's underplayed as a risk given it could invalidate the documented "expected: HTTP-plane PASS" result. Worth watching closely on the first real run.

### 3. Single source of truth (`BYPASS` constant) — holds, verified by simulation

Line 34 of the real `appctl_lib.py` is exactly `GOLDEN = "apphost-golden"`. I inserted `BYPASS = "apphost-bypass"` immediately after it (as the plan specifies) and ran the plan's exact awk command against the resulting file:
```
GOLDEN=[apphost-golden]
BYPASS=[apphost-bypass]
```
Identical extraction mechanism, confirmed working. No existing `BYPASS` symbol anywhere in the current file that could collide with the `^BYPASS = ` anchor.

### 4. `running=`/`stopped=` exclusion (lines 61–62, 76–77) — holds, correct minimal fix

Read verbatim:
```sh
running=$(orb list 2>/dev/null | awk '$1!="NAME" && $2=="running" {print $1}' \
          | grep -v '^docker$' | grep -v "^$GOLDEN$")
...
machines=${*:-$running}
neighbours=$running
...
stopped=$(orb list 2>/dev/null | awk '$1!="NAME" && $2!="running" {print $1}' \
          | grep -v '^docker$' | grep -v "^$GOLDEN$")
```
Appending `| grep -v "^$BYPASS$"` to both mirrors the existing GOLDEN-exclusion exactly (same shape, third pipe stage). No unintended interaction with line 68's arg-narrowing: with no args, `machines` (and `neighbours`) now skip BYPASS from the default set, exactly as GOLDEN already is skipped. Explicit-argument invocation (`check-isolation apphost-bypass`) still bypasses the `$running`-based exclusion entirely — but that's pre-existing behavior identical to how `check-isolation apphost-golden` already works today, not a new side effect introduced by this change.

### 5. design.md wording (§5) — holds

Read both files in full. `ingress-identity-cannot-be-borrowed/design.md` decision 8 (lines 333–334) already contains the precedent format: `**Resolved 2026-08-08:** relax the contract.` — the plan's proposed sentence for the sibling file, `**Resolved 2026-08-08: dedicated machine kept stopped, started only for the check** (per Joe).`, matches this exact shape: states the decision plainly, no "X rather than Y" comparison, no invented "because" beyond what's attributed to Joe. Confirmed the two currently-open cross-references the plan says to update both still say "owned by `only-owner-devices-open-a-shell` decision 4" and treat it as open (decision 8's resolution paragraph, lines 336–338, and the Open Questions bullet, lines 342–344) — matches the plan's described starting state, and the proposed pointer-only fix matches the same authoritative-source-plus-pointer pattern already used bidirectionally between these two files.

Minor caveat: I could not find any in-repo record of the "Cycle 2" precedent the revision note cites twice (grepped both change directories, the whole repo, and git log for "Cycle 2" — no hits). Likely an out-of-band conversation with Joe not captured in a tracked file; I can only confirm the proposed wording's *shape* matches the in-repo precedent I could find, not the origin of the rule itself.

### Bottom line

4 of 5 points hold as designed. Point 1 has a genuine, empirically-confirmed gap: the trap restores fleet state correctly but does not stop the script on an actual interrupt, which the plan's own live-fleet test (§6) is not positioned to catch since it only checks restoration. Recommend fixing the INT/TERM trap to explicitly `exit` after cleanup before running §6's live verification, so the interrupt test proves both properties (state restored *and* the run actually stops) rather than just one.

## Change 1 (Critical): consolidate cache-input assembly, wiring BOTH paths

Create one shared unexported function in internal/runner/runner.go:

```go
// collectCacheInputs assembles the cache-key inputs for a module build: the
// tagged files plus the module's own files and any filesystem replace-target
// files, so every bootstrap path shares one invalidation contract.
func collectCacheInputs(taggedFiles []discover.TaggedFile, importRoot string) ([]discover.TaggedFile, error) {
	moduleFiles, err := collectModuleFiles(importRoot)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("gathering module files: %w", err)
	}

	replaceFiles, err := collectReplaceDirFiles(importRoot)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("gathering replace target files: %w", err)
	}

	return slices.Concat(taggedFiles, moduleFiles, replaceFiles), nil
}
```

## Gate B — DESIGN-FIT Review: `5db8805` (bound `runGroupParallelAll` with a semaphore)

**Engram query run first** (`--phrase "go semaphore bounded concurrency channel idiom" --phrase "targ parallel runner design conventions"`). No prior lesson specific to a semaphore idiom existed in the vault; the closest applicable hit was note **401** (`targ-dep-execution-prior-art-and-code-map`), which names `runDeps` (target.go ~:497) dispatching to `runGroupParallelAll` / `runGroupParallel` / `runGroupSerial` — used to orient the surrounding-code inspection and confirmed accurate against the current diff. Note **131**/**226** (parallel-test-isolation: no shared mutable state across `t.Parallel()` subtests) was checked against the new test — the new test's shared vars (`cur`, `maxSeen`, `ran`) live inside a single, self-contained subtest (not shared across sibling parallel subtests), so the lesson doesn't apply here; no violation.

### Verdict: **PASS**

### What I checked
- Full diff (`internal/core/target.go`, `internal/core/target_internal_test.go`) against surrounding code: `runGroupParallel` (uncapped sibling, lines 790–909), `runGroupSerial`, `parallelCap` (line 767, pre-existing from commit `0a5c986`, unchanged here).
- `git show 0a5c986:.../target.go` vs `5db8805` to confirm `parallelCap` and its test table (incl. `ZeroTargetsCapsAtZero`) predate this task and are untouched.
- Codebase-wide grep for existing semaphore/`errgroup`/`x/sync` usage — none in project code; `golang.org/x/sync` is only an `// indirect` transitive dep in `go.mod`.
- Test-file conventions: `WithExecInfo(context.Background(), ExecInfo{Output: &buf})` matches the existing pattern in `print_test.go`; no other `makeTarget`-style helper exists elsewhere to diverge from.
- The governing plan (`docs/plans/2026-07-23-issue-26-dep-fanout-cap.md`, Task 2 of 9) — the diff is a verbatim implementation of the reviewed Task 2 spec, including the exact `max(1, capN)` clamp and test.

### Findings by question

1. **Semaphore integration** — clean, not bolted on. `sem` is declared in the same setup block as `resultCh`/`results` (natural top-to-bottom construction order), and the acquire/defer-release pair is the *first two statements* in the goroutine, followed by a blank line before the pre-existing body — so `OnStart` only fires once a slot is actually held (correct observability semantics), and there's no duplicated acquire logic anywhere else in the file. The change to the goroutine body is a 2-line insertion into an otherwise-untouched block.

2. **`max(1, capN)` clamp placement** — defensible SRP, correctly homed. `parallelCap`'s own test table (`ZeroTargetsCapsAtZero`) fixes its contract: 0 is a *meaningful* answer for zero targets, not a bug to be floored away. Forcing the floor into `parallelCap` would corrupt that documented contract and require re-duplicating the clamp at every call site (already 2, per Task 3 next). The real invariant being protected — "a buffered channel of capacity 0 used as acquire/release self-deadlocks the only goroutine that would ever release it" — is a private implementation detail of how `runGroupParallelAll` happens to bound itself with a channel. Guarding it at the point that owns the channel is the right boundary.

3. **Naming** — consistent with file idiom. `sem`, `capN` match the file's established short/descriptive local-var style (`n`, `procs`, `idx`, `tctx`, `resultCh`). `makeTarget` is a function-scoped test factory closure (not a package-level helper) used once, for 5 structurally identical targets — normal Go idiom, not a naming departure.

4. **YAGNI/overbuild** — none. One channel, one acquire/release pair, one parameter, one call-site update; no new abstraction, no new dependency (`errgroup`/`x/sync/semaphore` are absent from the whole codebase, consistent with `x/sync` being merely an unused indirect dep). Test helper is minimally scoped to its single use.

5. **Asymmetry (`ParallelAll` capped, `runGroupParallel` not yet)** — justified beyond mere task ordering. `runGroupParallelAll` never cancels its context (`// Collect ALL results — no cancellation`, line 970), so bounding it needs nothing but the semaphore. `runGroupParallel` cancels on first error and, per the plan's Task 3, will need an added "skip queued targets after cancel" guard to preserve fail-fast semantics under a cap — real, function-specific complexity that legitimately doesn't belong in this commit. The diff is a scoped, verbatim match to the pre-agreed plan (Task 2 of 9), not an arbitrary partial application.

No refuting findings. The diff reads as if the semaphore had been part of the original `runGroupParallelAll` design.
